**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure team
**Re:** Recommendation on Q3 compute capacity planning

**Summary**

We are at a decision point on compute. Our inference cluster is running hot during peak hours, batch jobs are queuing, and the obvious instinct is to buy more hardware. After several weeks of measurement and modeling, our recommendation is to spend the next quarter improving utilisation of the hardware we already own, and to defer the capital purchase until we have exhausted the cheaper options. We believe this gets us most of the capacity we need at a fraction of the cost, and it keeps our options open in a hardware market that is moving fast.

**Where we actually stand**

Our fleet currently averages 41% GPU utilisation across the week, but that number hides the real problem: peaks hit 90%+ during business hours while overnight utilisation drops below 15%. We are not short of compute in aggregate; we are short of compute at specific times. Roughly a third of our capacity is effectively idle when nobody is using it, and our batch workloads — training runs, embedding refreshes, evaluation sweeps — are competing with interactive traffic for the same machines.

This is a scheduling problem at least as much as a capacity problem. Batch jobs are latency-tolerant by nature; interactive inference is not. Moving batch work into the overnight trough, and putting aggressive autoscaling and queue-based admission control in front of interactive traffic, should flatten our peak substantially. Our modeling suggests these changes alone could absorb projected demand growth for two to three quarters.

**The cost picture**

The purchase option is expensive in more ways than the invoice. Eight high-end GPUs cost roughly $250K upfront, plus colocation, power, cooling, and the ongoing operational burden of managing more machines — a small team feels every additional node keenly. There is also a hidden cost we should be honest about: hardware bought today will likely be worth half as much in eighteen months, because the performance curve in this market is brutal. Capital deployed now is capital that depreciates quickly and cannot easily be redeployed.

By contrast, the utilisation work is mostly engineering time we would spend anyway. Queueing infrastructure, better scheduling, and quantisation or batching improvements to our serving stack are projects with value independent of this decision. Even if we do eventually buy hardware, this work makes the fleet we buy cheaper to run and the fleet we own more useful.

**Latency and reliability**

The counterargument deserves a fair hearing. Utilisation improvements are not free of risk. Packing more work onto existing machines raises the stakes when something fails: a node at 85% utilisation that dies takes more throughput with it than one loafing at 40%. Our current redundancy posture is thin — we have enough spare capacity to survive one node failure comfortably, and pushing utilisation up erodes that buffer. Any utilisation push must explicitly preserve headroom for failure, which means targeting perhaps 70% sustained peak rather than the theoretical maximum.

Latency is the other constraint. Higher utilisation means longer queues, and tail latency for interactive requests degrades nonlinearly as machines fill up. We can manage this with priority queues and careful admission control, but it is real engineering work with real failure modes, and we should not pretend it is a free lunch.

**Reversibility and opportunity cost**

This is the strongest argument for waiting. Hardware purchases are close to irreversible at our scale — we cannot resell quickly or cheaply, and we cannot un-spend the cash. Utilisation improvements are fully reversible: if a scheduling change hurts latency, we roll it back in an afternoon. In a market where GPU prices are softening, inference efficiency is improving quarter over quarter, and next-generation hardware keeps arriving, the option value of waiting is genuinely high. Every quarter we defer the purchase, the purchase we eventually make is likely to be better and cheaper.

The opportunity cost cuts the other way, too. Engineering time spent on scheduling infrastructure is time not spent on product work. But we judge that cost lower than a quarter-million dollars of rapidly depreciating capital, particularly since the scheduling work pays off regardless of what we later buy.

**Recommendation and honest uncertainty**

Spend the next quarter on utilisation: batch-to-overnight migration, queue-based admission control, and serving-stack efficiency work, with explicit headroom targets for reliability. Reassess the purchase at the end of the quarter with real post-change data.

We want to be clear about what we do not know. Our demand forecast has wide error bars; a large customer win could invalidate the two-to-three-quarter runway we project. And utilisation gains always look better in models than in production. If we hit 70% sustained utilisation and are still queuing, we should buy without further debate — and we should pre-approve that decision now so we are not re-litigating it under pressure later.

Happy to walk through the utilization data and cost model in Thursday's review.
